text: Mohinder Amarnath Bhardwaj, born on 24 September 1950 in Patiala, is a former Indian cricketer and cricket analyst, son of Lala Amarnath, the first post-independence captain of India. He served as vice-captain of the Indian team that won the 1983 Cricket World Cup, where he was named Player of the Final and also played a key role in the semi-final, earning Man of the Match honors in both matches. He was part of the Indian squad that won the 1985 World Championship of Cricket. Known widely by players and pundits as the best Indian batsman against express pace, Mohinder received the C. K. Nayudu Lifetime Achievement Award in 2009. He was the second eldest son of Lala Amarnath and Kailash Kumari; his elder brother Surinder was a former international cricketer, younger brother Rajinder a former first-class cricketer, and he has two sisters, Kamala and Dolly. He completed his schooling at MB High School, Mandir Marg, Delhi, and graduated from SGTB Khalsa College, Delhi University. Making his Test debut against Australia in December 1969 as a quick-bowling all-rounder, he was a top-order batsman, primarily playing at No. 3, known for being both attacking and defensive, and for reinventing his game over time. He was also skilled with the ball, bowling swingers and cutters with great control and had a unique run-up where he slowed down as he approached the crease. He played 69 Tests, scoring 4,378 runs at an average of 42.50, including 11 hundreds and 24 fifties, and took 32 wickets at 55.68; in 85 One Day Internationals, he scored 1,924 runs at an average of 30.53, with a highest score of 102 not out, and took 46 wickets at 42.84. Imran Khan of Pakistan and Malcolm Marshall of the West Indies praised his batsmanship, courage, and ability to endure pain. In the 1982–83 series against Pakistan and the West Indies, he scored over 1000 runs in the two series, and despite India losing the first three Tests 3–0, he was the sole saving grace for the batting line-up. Sunil Gavaskar, in his book "Idols," described Mohinder as the finest batsman in the world, and Imran Khan stated in his book "All Round View" that Mohinder was the best batsman in the world during the 1982–83 season and should have played continuously from his debut in 1969 until retirement. The series saw Imran Khan take 40 wickets and jointly win "Man of the Series" with Mohinder, who was instrumental in stabilizing India's batting. Sunil Gavaskar scored 434 runs in one innings during the series. Mohinder made his first Test century at Perth against Jeff Thomson at the WACA, the fastest and bounciest wicket in the world, and followed it with 10 more centuries against top-class fast bowling. In the 1983 World Cup semi-final against England, his accurate seam bowling led to the dismissal of David Gower and Mike Gatting, with only 27 runs given in 12 overs (2.25 per over), the lowest among Indian bowlers, and he scored 46 runs to provide a solid foundation, earning Man of the Match. In the final against the West Indies, India was dismissed for 183 in 54.4 overs, far below the 60-over target, but Amarnath's calm batting provided stability, occupying the crease for 80 balls and scoring 26 runs. Krishnamachari Srikkanth top-scored with 38, followed by Sandeep Patil with 27. India's chances were slim, but the Indian bowling, exploiting weather and pitch conditions, bowled out the West Indies for 140, winning by 43 runs. Amarnath and Madan Lal were joint highest wicket-takers with 3 wickets each, and he was again named Man of the Match for his economical bowling, conceding only 12 runs in 7 overs (1.71 per over), and also took the match-winning wicket. As vice-captain, he held the World Cup aloft in a famous photograph with captain Kapil Dev. Except for 1982–83, Mohinder never held a steady place in the Indian Test side and was frequently dropped, earning the nickname "Comeback Man" of Indian cricket. He was known for his batting technique, temperament, and skill, having experimented with a side-on batting stance. He was admired for his personality, courage, and determination; Vivian Richards called him "one of the nicest men to have ever played the game," and David Boon said "Concede didn't seem to be in his vocabulary." Gideon Haigh noted that despite being hit by Richard Hadlee, Imran Khan, Malcolm Marshall, and Jeff Thomson—suffering a skull fracture, being knocked unconscious, teeth knocked out, and a painful jaw injury—he never stopped hooking and continued playing, with Michael Holding stating that what separated him from others was his ability to withstand pain. During the Bridgetown Test in 1982–83, he retired for stitches after being hit on the head and returned to face Michael Holding, hooking a bouncer to the boundary. However, during the 1983/84 tour of India, the West Indies attack restricted him to just 1 run in six innings, with Holding dismissing him three times for ducks, leading to his drop shortly after his 1983 World Cup success. He played a key role in a famous chase at Queen's Park Oval, Port of Spain, in 1976, scoring 85 in the second innings to take India to the brink of a historic win. He had notable conflicts with the Indian cricket selectors, famously calling them a "bunch of jokers," which often led to his exclusion. Mohinder is the only Indian to be dismissed on handling the ball, first in an ODI on 9 February 1986, and the only Indian to be dismissed for obstructing the field in ODIs; he is also the only international cricketer to have been given out for both handling the ball and obstructing the field. He carried a red handkerchief visibly in his trouser pocket while batting as a superstition. He presented a popular weekly cricket coaching TV program in the late 80s and early 90s titled "Cricket with Mohinder Amarnath," which featured technique presentations and guest speakers, mostly from the Indian national team, and gained a strong following among youth, especially after the 1987 Reliance Cup, broadcast on Doordarshan. The program's title song, "Khel hi hain hamara jeevan...", was very catchy; young Sachin Tendulkar, at 15, was interviewed by Amarnath and later joined the Indian team for the Pakistan tour after a year. Mohinder is married to Inderjit Amarnath and has one daughter. The 2021 Hindi film 83, based on India's 1983 World Cup victory, features Saqib Saleem as Amarnath and Amarnath himself as his father, Lala, and he also played the role of a cricket coach to Saleem's character, Viraj Sharma, in the 2016 film Dishoom.
